summary: This informational memo documents a MAPOS version 1 extension, the Switch-Switch Protocol, which provides dynamic routing for unicast, broadcast and multicast traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2174 describes SSP, a routing extension for MAPOS networks with several switches. Switches exchange routes for unicast traffic and use a shared spanning tree to forward broadcast and multicast frames.

questions: what is the mapos switch-switch protocol
subtitle: Dynamic unicast and broadcast routing between MAPOS switches.

tldr.problem: MAPOS networks with multiple switches need a way to route unicast traffic and deliver broadcast or multicast frames without forwarding loops.
tldr.mechanism: SSP exchanges distance-vector routes for unicast and builds a spanning tree rooted at the lowest-numbered switch for broadcast and multicast.
tldr.outcome: This Informational memo documents a MAPOS version 1 extension; its forwarding rules and timers address the protocol's missing source-address and TTL fields.

today: RFC 2174 is an Informational memo published in June 1997, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It documents the Switch-Switch Protocol as an extension to MAPOS version 1.

sections.title: The Switch-Switch Protocol
sections.content:
MAPOS carries network-protocol packets in HDLC frames over SONET/SDH, with SONET switches providing access for connected nodes. The Switch-Switch Protocol (SSP) is a dynamic routing extension for a MAPOS version 1 network that spans multiple switches.

SSP uses distance-vector routing for unicast frames and a spanning-tree method for broadcast and multicast. MAPOS version 1 frames have no source address field and no Time To Live (TTL) field to limit forwarding loops, so the memo defines a virtual source switch and a forwarding delay for the broadcast and multicast method.
sections.plainLanguage: SSP lets MAPOS switches learn routes and forward traffic between them. It uses different rules for traffic sent to one destination and traffic sent to many destinations.

sections.title: MAPOS Addresses
sections.content:
A MAPOS node address is 8 bits and contains a switch number and a port number. The switch and port portions have variable lengths, and the least significant bit is always 1 as the address-field terminator. A most significant bit of 0 indicates a unicast address.

A most significant bit of 1 indicates broadcast or multicast. The broadcast address contains all 1s; for multicast, the remaining bits identify the group. The switch number tells a switch which destination switch the packet should reach.
sections.plainLanguage: A MAPOS address identifies a switch and a port on that switch. Its first bit distinguishes unicast from broadcast or multicast addressing.

sections.title: Unicast Routes and Route Updates
sections.content:
Each switch keeps a routing-table entry for each destination. An entry includes the destination, a subnet mask, a next-hop port and a metric representing distance. A metric of 1 means an adjacent switch; a metric of 16 means the destination is unreachable.

Switches exchange routing updates with adjacent switches every FULL_UPDATE_TIME, which defaults to 10 seconds. They add the link cost to received metrics and prefer a lower metric. Triggered updates send changed route information without waiting for the next periodic update. Split horizon with poisoned reverse advertises a route as unreachable to its next hop to reduce slow routing loops.
sections.plainLanguage: Each switch tracks the next hop and distance for destinations it can reach. It shares route changes with neighbors and can send an update immediately when a route fails.

sections.title: Broadcast and Multicast with VRPB
sections.content:
SSP uses Virtual Reverse Path Broadcast (VRPB) to build one spanning tree for broadcast and multicast. All such frames are treated as if they came from a Virtual Source Switch (VSS), the switch with the smallest switch number. Each switch uses its unicast routing information to determine its position relative to the VSS.

A switch forwards a broadcast or multicast frame to its upstream and downstream switches and directly connected nodes, but not back to the switch that sent the frame. After a new VSS is found, a forward-delay timer pauses forwarding while switches synchronize their routing information. Frames received on ports outside the upstream and downstream paths are discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: All switches use the lowest-numbered switch as the virtual root of one delivery tree. Each switch forwards frames along that tree without sending them back where they arrived.

sections.title: SSP Routing Messages
sections.content:
SSP packets are carried in the Information field of a MAPOS HDLC frame, using protocol value 0xFE05. The packet has a four-octet header followed by route entries. The command is one octet: value 1 requests routing information, and value 2 carries a response or update. The version field is one octet and has value 1 in this memo.

A packet can be at most 512 octets and can contain from 1 to 25 route entries. Each route entry is 20 octets. Periodic responses contain the routing table, while a triggered update can contain only changed entries.
sections.plainLanguage: SSP request messages ask for routes, and response messages carry routes. The memo limits packet size and the number of route entries in one packet.
